record.summary: The OECD's framework for organisations developing, deploying or providing advanced AI systems to report publicly on their alignment with the G7 Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct. Built around the Code's 11 actions, its questionnaire covers risk identification and evaluation, risk management and information security, transparency on advanced AI systems, governance and incident management, content authentication and provenance, and research on AI safety. Participation is voluntary and reports are published in full on OECD.AI.
record.notes: Launched on 7 February 2025 as an outcome of the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, after the G7 Digital and Tech Working Group under the Italian Presidency, following the Trento Declaration, asked the OECD to develop mechanisms for monitoring voluntary adoption of the Code. The OECD counts 25 reports in the first round, analysed in its 2025 report 'How are AI developers managing risks?'; MIC Japan's HAIP site says the first responses, from 19 companies, were published in April 2025. Version 2.0, launched on 28 May 2026 at a Tech7 event in Paris on the margins of the G7 Digital and Tech Ministerial under the French Presidency, distinguishes model developers, application developers and deployers and is simplified for small and medium enterprises; 31 reports under it were published on 2 October 2026. Organisations must be based in an OECD member, a GPAI member or an Adherent to the OECD Recommendation on AI.

verification.note: Stored: the OECD's Reporting Framework pages on OECD.AI (overview, about, list of reports with two of the reports published on 2 Oct 2026) and its announcement of version 2.0, all on 17 Oct 2026, and MIC Japan's Hiroshima AI Process page on the framework (11 Oct 2026). They give the launch on 7 February 2025, the G7 mandate, the framework's structure, the voluntary nature of reporting, the version 2.0 launch on 28 May 2026 (the announcement is dated 29 May 2026; the sentence on the launch gives the day without the year) and the 31 reports published on 2 October 2026. The February 2025 OECD press release on oecd.org refuses the archiver (HTTP 403), so the record's official URL is now the OECD.AI overview. The first-round count differs between the OECD (25 reports) and MIC (19 companies); both are in the notes. The blank questionnaire is a Word file and was not stored; its sections are taken from a published report.

title.quote: The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework, launched in February 2025, provides a standardised structure for organisations to report on their alignment with the Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems.
It builds on the Hiroshima AI Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems

date_published.quote: The Reporting Framework, launched on February 7 2025, is a direct outcome of the G7 Hiroshima AI Process
The Reporting Framework, launched on February 7, 2025, is a direct outcome of the G7 Hiroshima AI Process

date_last_updated.quote: On 28 May, the OECD launched version 2.0 of the Hiroshima AI Process (HAIP) Reporting Framework at an event organised by Tech7, on the margins of the G7 Digital and Tech Ministerial Meeting under the French G7 Presidency in Paris.

status.quote: Submissions are accepted on a rolling basis, and organisations are invited to update their reports annually.

On 28 May, the OECD launched Version 2.0 of the Hiroshima AI Process (HAIP) Reporting Framework.

legal_force.quote: Participation in this Reporting Framework is voluntary and does not constitute compliance with, or equivalence to, other frameworks
